name: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz and algebraic geometry as ideal theory
summary: Hilbert linked ideals of polynomials to geometric zero sets, starting the algebraisation of algebraic geometry.

name: Algebraic topology: Betti numbers to homology groups
summary: Numerical invariants (Betti numbers) of manifolds from the study of integrals and differential equations are replaced by groups, so algebra becomes the language of topology.

name: Representation theory of finite groups
summary: Frobenius, Burnside and Schur studied groups through matrix representations, and character tables proved structural theorems such as Burnside's p^a q^b.

name: p-adic numbers
summary: Hensel treated integers like power series in a prime, giving p-adic numbers, and Kuerschak and Hasse later turned this into valuation theory and local-global principles.

name: Representations of compact and continuous groups (Schur, Weyl, Peter-Weyl)
summary: Schur and Weyl used invariant integration to extend finite-group representation theory to compact Lie groups.

name: Burnside's use of character theory for finite group theory
summary: Burnside applied Frobenius characters to prove the p^a q^b solvability theorem.

name: Measure theory meets probability (Kolmogorov)
summary: Probability is axiomatised as a normalised measure on a sigma-algebra, so limit theorems become statements about integration.

name: Borel sets and measure
summary: Borel introduced a hierarchy of sets generated from open sets and applied countable additivity.

name: Lebesgue measure and integral: set theory enters analysis
summary: Lebesgue defined measure in 1901 and the integral in 1902 using Cantor-style set concepts, showing analysis required set-theoretic methods.

name: Hilbert's programme
summary: Hilbert proposed to prove consistency of mathematics by finitary methods.
